prompt: whats the actual difference between a metaphor and a simile
reply: A simile keeps a safety rail — like or as — so it stays an open comparison: the traffic moved like treacle. A metaphor removes the rail and simply asserts it: the traffic was treacle. Same image, different force ⚡ Metaphor hits harder because the reader makes the leap themselves. Write one of your own both ways and see which lands.[CHIPS]Mine is ready|What about personification|Mixed metaphors?[/CHIPS]

prompt: is it wrong to end a sentence with a preposition

prompt: what is passive voice and why do teachers hate it
reply: Active: the council fixed the road. Passive: the road was fixed. Notice who quietly vanished 🔍 Passive lets you drop the doer, which makes it a tool rather than a crime — science writing uses it on purpose, and mistakes were made is how blame gets hidden. Teachers push back when it just makes writing vague. Hunt for one in a news headline today.[CHIPS]Found one|Make mine active|When passive helps[/CHIPS]

prompt: what is a semicolon for

prompt: why is english spelling so weird compared to tamil

English froze many spellings around the time printing spread, then carried on changing how it spoke 📚 Add borrowed words that kept their original look — ballet from French, yacht from Dutch — and you get today's mess. English spelling is a fossil record.[FACT]Catamaran comes from Tamil kattumaram, meaning tied wood.[/FACT][CHIPS]More fossil words|Tamil words in english|What changed sounds[/CHIPS]

prompt: does the oxford comma actually matter
reply: Sometimes it decides the meaning. I thanked my parents, Rahul and Divya reads as though your parents ARE Rahul and Divya. Add the comma — my parents, Rahul, and Divya — and suddenly there are four people 🧩 It is named after Oxford University Press, which kept using it. Many British and Indian style guides drop it unless it prevents confusion. Pick a side and be consistent.[CHIPS]I'm pro comma|I'll skip it|Other comma traps[/CHIPS]

prompt: affect vs effect i never get it right

Learn the default cold, and deal with the exception only when you actually meet it.[CHIPS]Test me|Show the exception|Other confusable pairs[/CHIPS]

prompt: whats the difference between i ate and i have eaten
reply: I ate at four pins the action to a finished moment. I have eaten refuses to name a time, because it is really telling you about now: I am not hungry 🍽️ That is present perfect — past event, present relevance. It is also why I have eaten yesterday sounds off; yesterday is a closed box. Try both with finish my homework.[CHIPS]I have finished|I finished yesterday|More tense pairs[/CHIPS]

prompt: what is a dangling modifier

prompt: why do people say literally when they dont mean it
reply: Because intensifiers wear out. Really, truly and very all began as words meaning genuinely-true, then got spent on emphasis 🔁 Literally is simply the newest word on that treadmill, and writers have been stretching it for well over a century. Descriptively it is normal drift; in an exam, still use it strictly. Language changes, marks do not.[CHIPS]Other drifted words|Descriptive vs prescriptive|Is drift bad[/CHIPS]

prompt: what makes a sentence a run on
reply: A run-on welds two complete sentences together with nothing strong enough between them: I missed the bus I walked. The comma splice is its sibling: I missed the bus, I walked ✍️ You have four repairs — full stop, semicolon, a joining word like so, or a comma plus that word. Length is not the fault; a long sentence can be perfectly built. Repair mine your way.[CHIPS]So I walked|Semicolon version|Long correct example[/CHIPS]

prompt: what is alliteration and why bother

Your ear registers it before your brain does, so the phrase sticks 🔊 That is why headlines and brand names lean on it — it buys memory for free. prompt: is using they for one person correct

Major style guides accept it now. Read the sentence aloud with each option and pick the one nobody stumbles over.[CHIPS]They sounds best|More disputed rules|Why it changed[/CHIPS]
